short: Agincourt, the conquest of Normandy, and a claim to France that outlived him by weeks.
full:
Henry V inherited a throne his father had usurped and a reputation for competence earned fighting Welsh rebels. In 1415 he renewed the French war, took Harfleur, and on 25 October destroyed a much larger French army at Agincourt, where dismounted men-at-arms and massed longbowmen fought on a narrow, waterlogged field.

Agincourt made his name, but the systematic conquest of Normandy between 1417 and 1419 did the real work. With France split between Armagnac and Burgundian factions, the Treaty of Troyes in 1420 recognised Henry as heir to Charles VI and regent of France, sealed by his marriage to Catherine of Valois. He died of dysentery at Vincennes on 31 August 1422, aged 35, two months before the French king he was to succeed. His own heir was nine months old, and everything won in France was lost within thirty years.
